title: Genesis 19. The Cup of Fire.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 19. The Cup of Fire.
Two angels arrive at Sodom in the evening.
Lot is sitting in the gate, the place of judgment,
the place where a citizen of the city takes his seat among its elders.
Lot has moved from a tent near Sodom in chapter thirteen to a house inside Sodom.
The man who chose the well-watered plain has put down roots in the city whose men were wicked,
great sinners against the Lord.
Lot sees the angels.
He rises.
He bows.
He insists they come to his house.
Stay the night.
Wash your feet.
He bakes unleavened bread.
They eat.
The Cup of hospitality,
the same cup Abraham poured under the oaks of Mamre in the previous chapter,
is now being poured in Sodom.
The same gesture.
The same bread.
But the house it is served in is surrounded.
Before they lie down, the men of the city surround the house.
Young and old.
All the people.
From every quarter.
They call to Lot:
Where are the men who came to you tonight?
Bring them out to us, that we may know them.
The Cup of Sodom is full.
The city Abraham interceded for,
where he asked God to spare it for ten righteous,
pours out its violence.
Not some of the men.
All of them.
From every quarter.
Young and old.
The city that looked like the garden of the Lord in chapter thirteen now shows what grew in the garden.
Lot goes out.
He shuts the door behind him.
He says: My brothers, do not act so wickedly.
I have two daughters who have not known a man.
Let me bring them out to you.
Do to them what seems good in your eyes.
Only do nothing to these men,
for they have come under the shelter of my roof.
The same pattern as chapter nine, Noah drunk, exposed,
a son who does not cover.
But here it is inverted.
Lot offers his daughters to protect his guests.
The man who was supposed to shelter his household offers his household to shelter strangers.
The Cup of hospitality has become a cup of sacrifice,
and the sacrifice is his own children.
The men of Sodom refuse.
Stand back!
This fellow came to sojourn among us,
and now he appoints himself as a judge.
We will deal worse with you than with them.
They press hard against Lot.
They come near to break the door.
The angels reach out their hands, pull Lot inside,
and shut the door.
They strike the men at the door, small and great, with blindness.
The men grope.
They wearied themselves trying to find the door.
Even blinded, they still grope for the door.
The violence does not stop when the eyes are taken.
The Cup of Sodom is so full that blindness cannot restrain it.
The same word used for the men who grope in the dark is the word for those who seek God,
but here it is turned inside out.
They grope, but not for God.
For the door.
To break it.
To reach the ones inside.
The angels say to Lot: Do you have anyone else here?
Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, whoever you have in the city, bring them out.
For we are about to destroy this place.
The outcry before the Lord has grown great.
The Lord has sent us to destroy it.
Lot goes out to his sons-in-law,
the men pledged to marry his daughters.
Get up!
Get out of this place!
The Lord is about to destroy the city!
But he seems to his sons-in-law to be joking.
The word is the same root as Isaac, laughter.
Lot's warning sounds like laughter.
The man who has lived so long in Sodom that he sits at its gate cannot be taken seriously when he says it is about to burn.
The Cup of warning is poured,
and the ones who should drink it think it is a joke.
Morning comes.
The angels urge Lot: Get up!
Take your wife and your two daughters who are here,
lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.
But he lingered.
He lingered.
The man who was rescued from captivity by Abram in chapter fourteen now cannot leave the city that is about to burn.
He knows it will burn.
He has been told.
And he lingers.
The Cup that was offered to him, escape, life, freedom,
is met with delay.
The men seize his hand, his wife's hand,
and the hands of his two daughters.
The Lord being merciful to him.
They bring him out and set him outside the city.
Escape for your life.
Do not look back.
Do not stay in the plain.
Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed.
Lot says: Not so, my lord.
Your servant has found favor.
You have shown great kindness in saving my life.
But I cannot escape to the mountains,
lest evil overtake me and I die.
See, this city is near.
It is a little one.
Let me escape there.
Is it not a little one?
My soul will live.
The man who was told to run to the mountains bargains for a small city.
The same pattern as Abraham's intercession, but smaller.
Where Abraham asked God to spare a city for the righteous,
Lot asks God to spare a city for himself.
The angel grants it.
I will not overthrow the city you have spoken of.
Hurry.
Escape there, for I can do nothing until you arrive.
The city is named Zoar, Little.
The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar.
Then the Lord rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire,
from the Lord out of heaven.
He overthrew those cities.
All the plain.
All the inhabitants.
Everything that grew on the ground.
The Cup of fire.
What the flood did with water in chapter seven,
Sodom receives with fire.
The same God who opened the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven now opens heaven and pours out sulfur and fire.
The plain that looked like the garden of the Lord in chapter thirteen,
well-watered, lush, abundant, is now a furnace.
The garden is burned.
The abundance that Lot saw and chose is turned to ash.
But Lot's wife looked back.
From behind him.
She became a pillar of salt.
The Cup of fire takes the one who could not let go of what was being burned.
The woman who was seized by the hand and dragged out of the city could not stop looking back at it.
The command was: Do not look behind you.
She looked.
She became salt,
the same salt that covers the plain where the Dead Sea now sits.
The land that was like the garden of the Lord became a land where nothing grows,
where salt crystallizes on stone,
where a woman stands frozen in the act of longing for what God was destroying.
Abraham went up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the Lord.
He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah,
toward all the land of the plain.
He saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace.
The man who interceded stands silent.
He asked for fifty.
Then forty-five.
Forty.
Thirty.
Twenty.
Ten.
The answer was yes every time.
And now he sees the smoke.
Ten were not found.
The Cup of intercession was poured out.
The city was not spared.
Abraham does not speak.
The man who argued with God about justice stands before what justice looks like when there is no one left to spare it for.
When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham,
and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow.
God remembered Abraham.
Not Lot.
Abraham.
The same word used in chapter eight, God remembered Noah.
The memory of God is movement toward.
He remembered the man who interceded, and the remembering became rescue.
Lot was saved, not because Lot was righteous,
but because Abraham was remembered.
The Cup of intercession that seemed to fail, ten were not found,
actually succeeded.
It saved one man.
The one Abraham had been asking for all along.
Lot is afraid to stay in Zoar.
He goes to the mountains with his two daughters.
Into a cave.
His daughters speak: Our father is old.
There is no man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth.
Come, let us make our father drink wine, and lie with him,
that we may preserve offspring from our father.
The older daughter lies with her father.
He does not know when she lies down or when she rises.
The next night, the younger does the same.
Both conceive.
Moab is born.
Ben-Ammi is born.
Two nations, Moab and Ammon,
born in a cave from a father who did not know,
from daughters who believed the world had ended.
The Cup of fire leaves behind salt, two nations born of incest,
and a memory of what happens when the outcry is complete.
The man who chose the garden of the plain,
who moved his tent toward Sodom,
who sat in the gate of the city,
who offered his daughters to a mob,
who lingered when told to flee,
who bargained for a small city instead of the mountains,
ends in a cave.
The man Abraham rescued in chapter fourteen and God rescued in chapter nineteen cannot rescue himself.
He is pulled out by hands that are not his own.
Saved by mercy he did not earn.
Preserved because someone else was remembered.
The Cup of fire has been poured.
What it leaves behind is not life.
It is the remnants of life, a man in a cave,
two daughters who believe the world is empty,
two sons born from wine and darkness.
And Abraham, standing on a hillside,
watching smoke rise where a garden used to be.
